name: Linux — Anti-Forensics: File Immutability or Secure Deletion (chattr/shred)
description: Detects execution of chattr (setting/removing file immutability, often to protect malware or block log writes) or secure-deletion tools (shred/wipe/srm) used to destroy forensic evidence.
note:
## Investigation
1. `user.name` ran `process.executable` `process.args` on `host.name`.
2. `chattr +i` protects a file from modification; `shred` destroys it.
## Response
Preserve remaining evidence, identify the target files, and treat as active intrusion cleanup.
author: raadabujaish
query: event.category:"process" and process.name:("chattr" or "shred" or "wipe" or "srm")

name: Linux — at/batch Job Scheduling (Persistence)
description: Detects use of the 'at' / 'batch' one-shot job schedulers (0 baseline on these servers), used by attackers to schedule delayed or one-time execution of payloads for persistence or defence evasion.
note:
## Investigation
1. `user.name` scheduled a job via at/batch on `host.name`.
2. Inspect the scheduled command (atq/at -c).
## Response
Remove unauthorised jobs and investigate the user.
author: raadabujaish
query: event.category:"process" and process.name:("at" or "batch")

name: Linux — Attempt to Disable IPTables or Firewall
description: Adversaries may attempt to disable the iptables or firewall service in an attempt to affect how a host is allowed to receive or send network traffic.
author: raadabujaish

name: Linux — Bash Shell Profile Modification
description: Both ~/.bash_profile and ~/.bashrc are files containing shell commands that are run when Bash is invoked. These files are executed in a user's context, either interactively or non-interactively, when a user logs in so that their environment is set correctly. Adversaries may abuse this to establish persistence by executing malicious content triggered by a user’s shell.
author: raadabujaish
query:
event.category:file and event.type:change and
  process.name:(* and not (sudo or vim or zsh or env or nano or bash or Terminal or xpcproxy or login or cat or cp or
  launchctl or java or dnf or tailwatchd or ldconfig or yum or semodule or cpanellogd or dockerd or authselect or chmod or
  dnf-automatic or git or dpkg or platform-python)) and
  not process.executable:(/Applications/* or /private/var/folders/* or /usr/local/* or /opt/saltstack/salt/bin/*) and
  file.path:(/private/etc/rc.local or
             /etc/rc.local or
             /home/*/.profile or
             /home/*/.profile1 or
             /home/*/.bash_profile or
             /home/*/.bash_profile1 or
             /home/*/.bashrc or
             /Users/*/.bash_profile or
             /Users/*/.zshenv)

name: Linux — Container Escape Tooling Executed (nsenter/unshare/capsh)
description: Detects execution of namespace/capability manipulation tools (nsenter, unshare, capsh) commonly used to break out of a container to the host or to manipulate Linux namespaces for privilege escalation.
note:
## Investigation
1. `user.name` on `host.name` ran `process.executable` with `process.args`.
2. Determine whether the host is a container node and whether the invocation targets the host namespace/PID 1.
## Response
If unexpected, isolate the node and inspect the originating container/pod.
author: raadabujaish
query: event.category:"process" and process.name:("nsenter" or "unshare" or "capsh")

name: Linux — Creation of Hidden Files and Directories via CommandLine
description: Users can mark specific files as hidden simply by putting a "." as the first character in the file or folder name. Adversaries can use this to their advantage to hide files and folders on the system for persistence and defense evasion. This rule looks for hidden files or folders in common writable directories.
author: raadabujaish
query:
process where host.os.type == "linux" and event.type == "start" and event.action == "exec" and
process.working_directory in ("/tmp", "/var/tmp", "/dev/shm") and
process.args regex~ """\.[a-z0-9_\-][a-z0-9_\-\.]{1,254}""" and
not process.name in ("ls", "find", "grep", "git", "jq", "basename")

name: Linux — Credential File Modified (/etc/passwd, /etc/shadow, /etc/group)
description:
Attacker objective
Establish persistence or escalate privileges on a Linux host by adding a backdoor account, changing a password hash, or granting sudo rights — i.e., modifying the core credential and authorization files.

Attack logic
On Linux, /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow, /etc/group and /etc/sudoers define accounts, password hashes and privilege. An unexpected modification to these files can plant a backdoor user, reset a password, or grant elevated rights.

Why this detection works
File-integrity monitoring records write/rename events to these exact credential files, so any change to them is a high-signal, security-relevant event even without process context.

False positives
Legitimate user administration, password changes, or configuration-management/patch tooling that edits these files.

Tuning
Allowlist verified user-management and configuration-management workflows/hosts; prioritise servers where account changes are rare; correlate with the host's authentication and shell activity (which FIM does not capture).

Required telemetry
File Integrity Monitoring (fim.event): file.path, event.action, file.hash, host.name. Note: FIM does not record the process or user that made the change.
author: raadabujaish
note:
## Investigation guide
1. file.path identifies the credential file and host.name the system; FIM does not show who or which process changed it.
2. Pivot to the host's auth/shell logs (system.auth/auditd) to identify the actor and whether a backdoor account or sudo grant was added.
3. If unexplained, treat as persistence/privilege escalation and investigate the host.
false_positives: Legitimate user administration, password changes, or configuration-management/patch tooling that edits these files.
query: event.dataset:"fim.event" and event.action:("created" or "updated" or "moved") and file.path:("/etc/passwd" or "/etc/shadow" or "/etc/group" or "/etc/sudoers")

name: Linux — Cron Job File Created or Modified
description:
Attacker objective
Persist on a Linux host by creating or modifying a cron job that periodically executes attacker code.

Attack logic
Cron executes commands on a schedule from job files under /etc/cron* and the per-user spool. Creating or altering one of these files installs a recurring execution/persistence mechanism.

Why this detection works
File-integrity monitoring records writes to the cron job files, surfacing cron-based persistence at the filesystem level even without process context.

False positives
Legitimate administration or configuration-management tooling that installs/updates a cron job.

Tuning
Allowlist verified configuration-management and application-deployment workflows; correlate with the host's shell/auth activity (not captured by FIM); prioritise servers where cron rarely changes.

Required telemetry
File Integrity Monitoring (fim.event): file.path (cron job files), event.action, host.name. No process/user context — correlate with auditd.
author: raadabujaish
note:
## Investigation guide
1. file.path names the cron file and host.name the host; FIM does not show who added it.
2. Pivot to auditd/system.auth to identify the actor and the command scheduled.
3. Review the job's command; an unexpected cron entry is persistence — remove and investigate.
false_positives: Legitimate administration or configuration-management tooling that installs/updates a cron job.
query: event.dataset:"fim.event" and event.action:("created" or "updated" or "moved") and (file.path:"/etc/crontab" or file.path:"/etc/anacrontab" or file.path:*/etc/cron.d/* or file.path:*/etc/cron.hourly/* or file.path:*/etc/cron.daily/* or file.path:*/etc/cron.weekly/* or file.path:*/etc/cron.monthly/* or file.path:*/var/spool/cron/*)

name: Linux — Executable Masquerading as Kernel Process
description: Monitors for kernel processes with associated process executable fields that are not empty. Unix kernel processes such as kthreadd and kworker typically do not have process.executable fields associated to them. Attackers may attempt to hide their malicious programs by masquerading as legitimate kernel processes.
author: raadabujaish
query:
process where host.os.type == "linux" and event.type == "start" and event.action in ("exec", "exec_event") and
process.name : ("kworker*", "kthread*") and process.executable != null

name: Linux — Interactive Terminal Spawned via Perl
description: Identifies when a terminal (tty) is spawned via Perl. Attackers may upgrade a simple reverse shell to a fully interactive tty after obtaining initial access to a host.
author: raadabujaish
query:
event.category:process and host.os.type:linux and event.type:(start or process_started) and process.name:perl and
  process.args:("exec \"/bin/sh\";" or "exec \"/bin/dash\";" or "exec \"/bin/bash\";")

name: Linux — Masquerading Space After Filename
description: This rules identifies a process created from an executable with a space appended to the end of the filename. This may indicate an attempt to masquerade a malicious file as benign to gain user execution. When a space is added to the end of certain files, the OS will execute the file according to it's true filetype instead of it's extension. Adversaries can hide a program's true filetype by changing the extension of the file. They can then add a space to the end of the name so that the OS automatically executes the file when it's double-clicked.
author: raadabujaish
query:
process where host.os.type:("linux","macos") and
  event.type == "start" and
  (process.executable regex~ """/[a-z0-9\s_\-\\./]+\s""") and not
  process.name in ("ls", "find", "grep", "xkbcomp")

name: Linux — Modification of Dynamic Linker Preload Shared Object
description: Identifies modification of the dynamic linker preload shared object (ld.so.preload). Adversaries may execute malicious payloads by hijacking the dynamic linker used to load libraries.
author: raadabujaish
query:
host.os.type:linux and event.category:file and event.action:(updated or renamed or rename or file_rename_event) and 
not event.type:deletion and file.path:/etc/ld.so.preload and not process.name:(wine or oneagentinstallaction)

name: Linux — Netcat Listener Established via rlwrap
description: Monitors for the execution of a netcat listener via rlwrap. rlwrap is a 'readline wrapper', a small utility that uses the GNU Readline library to allow the editing of keyboard input for any command. This utility can be used in conjunction with netcat to gain a more stable reverse shell.
author: raadabujaish
query:
process where host.os.type == "linux" and event.type == "start" and event.action in ("exec", "exec_event") and 
process.name == "rlwrap" and process.args in ("nc", "ncat", "netcat", "nc.openbsd", "socat") and
process.args : "*l*" and process.args_count >= 4

name: Linux — Netcat/Socat Execution (Reverse Shell / Tunneling)
description: Detects execution of netcat/socat — frequently used to establish reverse shells, bind shells, or data-tunneling channels. These tools do not appear in normal application workloads on these servers.
note:
## Investigation
1. `user.name` ran `process.executable` `process.args` on `host.name`.
2. Look for `-e`, `exec`, or `/dev/tcp` patterns and the remote endpoint.
## Response
Isolate the host and identify the C2 destination and parent process.
author: raadabujaish
query: event.category:"process" and process.name:("nc" or "ncat" or "netcat" or "socat")

name: Linux — Network Activity Detected via Kworker
description: This rule monitors for network connections from a kworker process. kworker, or kernel worker, processes are part of the kernel's workqueue mechanism. They are responsible for executing work that has been scheduled to be done in kernel space, which might include tasks like handling interrupts, background activities, and other kernel-related tasks. Attackers may attempt to evade detection by masquerading as a kernel worker process.
author: raadabujaish
query:
host.os.type:linux and event.category:network and event.action:(connection_attempted or connection_accepted) and 
process.name:kworker* and not destination.ip:(
  10.0.0.0/8 or
  127.0.0.0/8 or
  169.254.0.0/16 or
  172.16.0.0/12 or
  192.168.0.0/16 or
  224.0.0.0/4 or
  "::1" or
  "FE80::/10" or
  "FF00::/8"
) and not destination.port:2049

name: Linux — Network Traffic Capture via CAP_NET_RAW
description: Identifies the ability of a process to be able to create RAW and PACKET socket types for the available network namespaces by a non-root user. A malicious process with this capability may exploit routing between hosts, bypass network access controls, and otherwise tamper with host networking if a firewall is not in place to limit the packet types and contents. The CAP_NET_RAW capability allows the process to bind to any address within the available namespaces, which allows network traffic sniffing by a non root user. The rule identifies previously unknown processes executing with CAP_NET_RAW capabilities through the use of the new terms rule type.
author: raadabujaish
query:
event.category:"process" and host.os.type:"linux" and event.type:"start" and event.action:"exec" and process.name:* and
(process.thread.capabilities.effective:"CAP_NET_RAW" or process.thread.capabilities.permitted:"CAP_NET_RAW") and
not user.id:"0"

name: Linux — pkexec Execution (PwnKit / Local Privilege Escalation)
description: Detects execution of pkexec, the setuid Polkit binary abused by PwnKit (CVE-2021-4034) and related local privilege-escalation exploits to obtain root. pkexec is not used by normal workloads on these servers (0 baseline).
note:
## Investigation
1. `user.name` ran `process.executable` `process.args` on `host.name`.
2. PwnKit exploitation often shows pkexec with empty/malformed argv and an unusual parent.
## Response
If unexpected, isolate the host, patch Polkit, and hunt for root-level persistence.
author: raadabujaish
query: event.category:"process" and process.name:"pkexec"

name: Linux — Potential Linux Credential Dumping via Unshadow
description: Identifies the execution of the unshadow utility which is part of John the Ripper, a password-cracking tool on the host machine. Malicious actors can use the utility to retrieve the combined contents of the '/etc/shadow' and '/etc/password' files. Using the combined file generated from the utility, the malicious threat actors can use them as input for password-cracking utilities or prepare themselves for future operations by gathering credential information of the victim.
author: raadabujaish
query:
process where host.os.type == "linux" and event.type == "start" and event.action in ("exec", "exec_event") and
process.name == "unshadow" and process.args_count >= 3

name: Linux — Potential Memory Seeking Activity
description: Monitors for the execution of Unix utilities that may be leveraged as memory address seekers. Attackers may leverage built-in utilities to seek specific memory addresses, allowing for potential future manipulation/exploitation.
author: raadabujaish
query:
process where host.os.type == "linux" and event.type == "start" and event.action in ("exec", "exec_event") and (
  (process.name == "tail" and process.args == "-c") or
  (process.name == "cmp" and process.args == "-i") or
  (process.name in ("hexdump", "xxd") and process.args == "-s") or
  (process.name == "dd" and process.args : ("skip*", "seek*"))
)

name: Linux — Potential Privilege Escalation via PKEXEC
description: Identifies an attempt to exploit a local privilege escalation in polkit pkexec (CVE-2021-4034) via unsecure environment variable injection. Successful exploitation allows an unprivileged user to escalate to the root user.
author: raadabujaish

subtechnique.name: Path Interception by PATH Environment Variable

query: file where host.os.type == "linux" and file.path : "/*GCONV_PATH*"

name: Linux — Potential Protocol Tunneling via EarthWorm
description: Identifies the execution of the EarthWorm tunneler. Adversaries may tunnel network communications to and from a victim system within a separate protocol to avoid detection and network filtering, or to enable access to otherwise unreachable systems.
author: raadabujaish
query:
process where host.os.type == "linux" and event.type == "start" and
 process.args : "-s" and process.args : "-d" and process.args : "rssocks"

name: Linux — Potential Upgrade of Non-interactive Shell
description: Identifies when a non-interactive terminal (tty) is being upgraded to a fully interactive shell. Attackers may upgrade a simple reverse shell to a fully interactive tty after obtaining initial access to a host, in order to obtain a more stable connection.
author: raadabujaish
query:
process where host.os.type == "linux" and event.type == "start" and event.action in ("exec", "exec_event") and (
  (process.name == "stty" and process.args == "raw" and process.args == "-echo" and process.args_count >= 3) or
  (process.name == "script" and process.args in ("-qc", "-c") and process.args == "/dev/null" and 
   process.args_count == 4)
)

name: Linux — Process Capability Enumeration
description: Identifies recursive process capability enumeration of the entire filesystem through the getcap command. Malicious users may manipulate identified capabilities to gain root privileges.
author: raadabujaish
query:
process where host.os.type == "linux" and event.type == "start" and event.action in ("exec", "exec_event") and
process.name == "getcap" and process.args == "-r" and process.args == "/" and process.args_count == 3 and
user.id != "0"

name: Linux — Scripted Password Change (chpasswd)
description: Detects execution of chpasswd, which sets account passwords non-interactively from a script or pipe — used by attackers to change or reset local account passwords for persistence or account takeover.
note:
## Investigation
1. `user.name` ran chpasswd on `host.name`.
2. Identify which account(s) had passwords changed.
## Response
Verify authorisation; if malicious, reset affected accounts and investigate.
author: raadabujaish
query: event.category:"process" and process.name:"chpasswd"

name: Linux — SELinux / Security Control Tampering (setenforce/semanage)
description: Detects execution of setenforce or semanage, used to place SELinux in permissive mode or alter its policy — a common step to disable a Linux security control before further attack activity.
note:
## Investigation
1. `user.name` ran `process.executable` `process.args` on `host.name`.
2. `setenforce 0` disables SELinux enforcement.
## Response
Re-enable enforcement, and investigate what activity followed the change.
author: raadabujaish
query: event.category:"process" and process.name:("setenforce" or "semanage")

name: Linux — Sensitive Files Compression
description: Identifies the use of a compression utility to collect known files containing sensitive information, such as credentials and system configurations.
author: raadabujaish
query:
event.category:process and host.os.type:linux and event.type:start and
  process.name:(zip or tar or gzip or hdiutil or 7z) and
  process.args:
    (
      /root/.ssh/id_rsa or
      /root/.ssh/id_rsa.pub or
      /root/.ssh/id_ed25519 or
      /root/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub or
      /root/.ssh/authorized_keys or
      /root/.ssh/authorized_keys2 or
      /root/.ssh/known_hosts or
      /root/.bash_history or
      /etc/hosts or
      /home/*/.ssh/id_rsa or
      /home/*/.ssh/id_rsa.pub or
      /home/*/.ssh/id_ed25519 or
      /home/*/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub or
      /home/*/.ssh/authorized_keys or
      /home/*/.ssh/authorized_keys2 or
      /home/*/.ssh/known_hosts or
      /home/*/.bash_history or
      /root/.aws/credentials or
      /root/.aws/config or
      /home/*/.aws/credentials or
      /home/*/.aws/config or
      /root/.docker/config.json or
      /home/*/.docker/config.json or
      /etc/group or
      /etc/passwd or
      /etc/shadow or
      /etc/gshadow
    )

name: Linux — Shared Object Created or Changed by Previously Unknown Process
description: This rule monitors the creation of shared object files by previously unknown processes. The creation of a shared object file involves compiling code into a dynamically linked library that can be loaded by other programs at runtime. While this process is typically used for legitimate purposes, malicious actors can leverage shared object files to execute unauthorized code, inject malicious functionality into legitimate processes, or bypass security controls. This allows malware to persist on the system, evade detection, and potentially compromise the integrity and confidentiality of the affected system and its data.
author: raadabujaish
query:
host.os.type:linux and event.action:(creation or file_create_event or file_rename_event or rename) and 
file.path:(/dev/shm/* or /usr/lib/*) and file.extension:so and process.name:* and not (
  process.name:("dockerd" or "dpkg" or "rpm" or "snapd" or "yum" or "vmis-launcher" or "pacman" or
  "apt-get" or "dnf" or "podman" or "platform-python") or 
  (process.name:vmware-install.pl and file.path:/usr/lib/vmware-tools/*)
)

name: Linux — Sudoers File Modification
description: A sudoers file specifies the commands that users or groups can run and from which terminals. Adversaries can take advantage of these configurations to execute commands as other users or spawn processes with higher privileges.
author: raadabujaish
query:
event.category:file and event.type:change and file.path:(/etc/sudoers* or /private/etc/sudoers*) and
not process.name:(dpkg or platform-python or puppet or yum or dnf) and 
not process.executable:(/opt/chef/embedded/bin/ruby or /opt/puppetlabs/puppet/bin/ruby or /usr/bin/dockerd)

name: Linux — Suspicious File Creation via Kworker
description: This rule monitors for a file creation event originating from a kworker parent process. kworker, or kernel worker, processes are part of the kernel's workqueue mechanism. They are responsible for executing work that has been scheduled to be done in kernel space, which might include tasks like handling interrupts, background activities, and other kernel-related tasks. Attackers may attempt to evade detection by masquerading as a kernel worker process.
author: raadabujaish
query:
file where host.os.type == "linux" and event.action in ("creation", "file_create_event") and
  process.name : "kworker*" and not (
    (process.name : "kworker*kcryptd*") or
    (file.path : ("/var/log/*", "/var/crash/*", "/var/run/*", "/var/lib/systemd/coredump/*", "/var/spool/*"))
  )

name: Linux — Suspicious Kworker UID Elevation
description: Monitors for the elevation of regular user permissions to root permissions through the kworker process. kworker, or kernel worker, processes are part of the kernel's workqueue mechanism. They are responsible for executing work that has been scheduled to be done in kernel space, which might include tasks like handling interrupts, background activities, and other kernel-related tasks. Attackers may attempt to evade detection by masquerading as a kernel worker process, and hijack the execution flow by hooking certain functions/syscalls through a rootkit in order to provide easy access to root via a special modified command.
author: raadabujaish
query:
process where host.os.type == "linux" and event.action == "session_id_change" and process.name : "kworker*" and
user.id == "0"

name: Linux — Suspicious Memory grep Activity
description: Monitors for grep activity related to memory mapping. The /proc/*/maps file in Linux provides a memory map for a specific process, detailing the memory segments, permissions, and what files are mapped to these segments. Attackers may read a process's memory map to identify memory addresses for code injection or process hijacking.
author: raadabujaish
query:
process where host.os.type == "linux" and event.type == "start" and event.action in ("exec", "exec_event") and
process.name in ("grep", "egrep", "fgrep", "rgrep") and process.args in ("[stack]", "[vdso]", "[heap]")

name: Linux — System Log File Deletion
description: Identifies the deletion of sensitive Linux system logs. This may indicate an attempt to evade detection or destroy forensic evidence on a system.
author: raadabujaish

subtechnique.name: Clear Linux or Mac System Logs

query:
file where host.os.type == "linux" and event.type == "deletion" and
  file.path :
    (
    "/var/run/utmp",
    "/var/log/wtmp",
    "/var/log/btmp",
    "/var/log/lastlog",
    "/var/log/faillog",
    "/var/log/syslog",
    "/var/log/messages",
    "/var/log/secure",
    "/var/log/auth.log",
    "/var/log/boot.log",
    "/var/log/kern.log"
    ) and
    not process.name in ("gzip", "executor", "dockerd")

name: Linux — Virtual Machine Fingerprinting
description: An adversary may attempt to get detailed information about the operating system and hardware. This rule identifies common locations used to discover virtual machine hardware by a non-root user. This technique has been used by the Pupy RAT and other malware.
author: raadabujaish
query:
event.category:process and host.os.type:linux and event.type:(start or process_started) and
  process.args:("/sys/class/dmi/id/bios_version" or
                "/sys/class/dmi/id/product_name" or
                "/sys/class/dmi/id/chassis_vendor" or
                "/proc/scsi/scsi" or
                "/proc/ide/hd0/model") and
  not user.name:root

name: Linux — Yum/DNF Plugin Status Discovery
description: This rule detects the execution of the `grep` command with the `plugins` argument on Linux systems. This command is used to search for YUM/DNF configurations and/or plugins with an enabled state. This behavior may indicate an attacker is attempting to establish persistence in a YUM or DNF plugin.
author: raadabujaish
query:
process where host.os.type == "linux" and event.type == "start" and event.action in ("exec", "exec_event") and
process.name == "grep" and process.args : "plugins*" and process.args : (
  "/etc/yum.conf", "/usr/lib/yum-plugins/*", "/etc/yum/pluginconf.d/*",
  "/usr/lib/python*/site-packages/dnf-plugins/*", "/etc/dnf/plugins/*", "/etc/dnf/dnf.conf"
)
